section.title: The Battle with Amalek
section.sectionRationale: Immediately after the rock gives water, Israel faces a fresh threat: Amalek's unprovoked attack at Rephidim. The battle becomes a living picture of the whole Christian life, human effort under Joshua's sword and dependence on God in Moses' raised hands, with Aaron and Hur holding him up when he grows weary.
section.thesis: Amalek attacks a weary, defenseless Israel, and victory comes only as Joshua fights below while Moses' hands, held up by Aaron and Hur, are lifted toward heaven above; the LORD Himself gets the credit and the altar's name, and the passage closes with the hard, honest language of covenant judgment against Amalek for generations to come.
section.frameNote: Three scenes: Amalek's attack and Moses' plan; the battle itself, won only as long as Moses' hands stay lifted with help from Aaron and Hur; and the aftermath, a written memorial, an altar named The LORD Is My Banner, and the sober word of ongoing judgment on Amalek.

verses.text: After this, the {{amalek|Amalekites}} came and attacked the Israelites at Rephidim.
So Moses said to Joshua, “Choose some of our men and go out to fight the Amalekites. Tomorrow I will stand on the hilltop with the staff of God in my hand.”

units.label: Hands lifted, hands held up
units.note: as long as Moses held up his hands, Israel prevailed

verses.text: Joshua did as Moses had instructed him and fought against the Amalekites, while Moses, Aaron, and Hur went up to the top of the hill.
As long as Moses held up his hands, Israel prevailed; but when he lowered them, Amalek prevailed.

When Moses’ hands grew heavy, they took a stone and put it under him, and he sat on it. Then Aaron and Hur held his hands up, one on each side, so that his hands remained steady until the sun went down.
So Joshua overwhelmed Amalek and his army with the sword.
Then the LORD said to Moses, “Write this on a scroll as a reminder and recite it to Joshua, because I will utterly blot out the memory of Amalek from under heaven.”
And Moses built an altar and named it {{banner|The LORD Is My Banner}}.
“Indeed,” he said, “a hand was lifted up toward the {{throne|throne}} of the LORD. The LORD will war against Amalek from generation to generation.”

amalek.gloss: Amalek, a grandson of Esau, Genesis 36:12, and so a distant kinsman turned enemy. His unprovoked attack on the weary and defenseless, Deuteronomy 25:17-18, marks Amalek as a byword for cruel opposition to God's redeemed people.

banner.gloss: My banner, my rallying standard. A nes was a raised signal by which scattered troops could see where to gather; naming the altar Yahweh Nissi, the LORD is my banner, Moses gives all credit for the victory to God rather than to Israel's own strength.

throne.gloss: Throne, here an unusual shortened form of the ordinary word kisse, forming a wordplay with Yah, the shortened divine name. The line is among the most compressed in the Hebrew Bible, but its sense is plain: this war belongs finally to the LORD.

basic.context: Fresh from water at the rock, Israel is attacked without warning by Amalek, distant kin through Esau, who strikes the weary and straggling at the rear, Deuteronomy 25:17-18. Moses sends Joshua to fight while he climbs the hill with the staff of God, and the battle turns entirely on whether his hands stay lifted.
basic.hermeneutics: This is real, remembered history, a specific battle at Rephidim, ordered to be written down so it would not be forgotten. It teaches, by its very structure, that human effort, Joshua's sword, and dependence on God, Moses' lifted hands upheld by others, belong together, not as competitors but as one whole obedience.
basic.originalLanguages: Amalek's name marks him as a kinsman turned enemy, grandson of Esau. Moses names the altar Yahweh Nissi, the LORD is my banner, my rallying point, refusing any credit for the victory. The closing line is famously compressed in Hebrew, a hand raised to the kes, throne, of Yah, language ancient readers already found difficult, but its thrust is plain: this war belongs to the LORD, not to Israel's strength.
basic.typology: Moses' raised hands, upheld to the very end of the battle by Aaron and Hur, anticipate the ongoing, unwearied intercession of Christ, our great high priest, who is never too weary to hold up His people, and who, unlike Moses, needs no one to hold up His hands.
basic.christ: Moses stands on the hill interceding while Joshua, whose name is the Hebrew form of Jesus, fights and wins the battle below; Scripture later shows the greater Joshua, Jesus, winning the decisive battle against sin and death while His people are carried by His unfailing intercession, Hebrews 7:25.
basic.god: God fights for His people through ordinary means, a sword in Joshua's hand and a staff in Moses', while making unmistakably clear that the victory and the glory are His alone; He also speaks in the hard language of covenant judgment against Amalek, showing that His patience with unprovoked cruelty toward His people is not unlimited.
basic.crossReferences: Deuteronomy 25:17-19 recalls Amalek's cowardly attack and commands Israel to remember and, in time, blot out his memory. 1 Samuel 15 shows Saul's failure to carry out that command. Hebrews 7:25 pictures Christ's unceasing intercession, of which Moses' upheld hands are a small, weary shadow. 1 Timothy 2:8 echoes lifted hands as the posture of prayer.
basic.oneStory: Israel's rescue is never finished with the exodus alone; it must be defended, generation after generation, against enemies who will not let God's redeemed people rest. The pattern set here, human effort joined to God given, God sustained intercession, points to Christ, who fights and prays for His people at once, and who will one day put every enemy, however old and however patient His judgment, finally under His feet.

context.literary:
Exodus 15:22 to 18:27 is a travel narrative that carries Israel from the sea to the mountain, and it is built from short, testing episodes: bitter water at Marah, bread from heaven, water from the rock, the Amalekite battle, and Jethro's visit. The first three are tests from within, hunger and thirst that expose grumbling hearts. The battle with Amalek is the first test from outside. It follows directly on the question that closes the Massah story, 'Is the LORD among us or not?' Exodus 17:7. The narrator lets the next verse answer it: an enemy arrives, and the LORD proves Himself present in the fight.

The passage falls into three scenes. Verses 8 and 9 set out the threat and the plan, verses 10 to 13 tell the battle, and verses 14 to 16 turn the victory into memory, worship and a standing sentence. The battle scene is built vertically, the hilltop above and the valley below, and the narrator cuts between them. Verse 11 is a tightly balanced pair of clauses, hands up and Israel prevails, hands down and Amalek prevails, and the whole outcome hangs on that swing.

One word runs through the passage like a thread. Moses will stand with the staff 'in my hand,' verse 9; his 'hands' are raised, lowered, grow heavy and are held, verses 11 and 12; and the closing saying speaks of 'a hand' lifted toward the throne of the LORD, verse 16. The hand of God that struck Egypt now works through a tired man's hands.

The chapter also sets up a contrast with what follows. Amalek, kin through Esau, comes to attack; in chapter 18 Jethro, a Midianite priest, comes to bless. Side by side they show the two ways the nations respond to the people God has redeemed, the pattern promised in Genesis 12:3.
context.historical:
Amalek appears in Genesis as a clan within Edom, the son of Esau's son Eliphaz by the concubine Timna, Genesis 36:12, and later counted among the chiefs of Eliphaz, Genesis 36:16. By the time of the exodus the Amalekites were a mobile people of the southern deserts. Numbers 13:29 places them in the Negev, and later texts show them raiding on the move, with camels, 1 Samuel 30:17. Their attack at Rephidim fits that way of life: not a siege or a set battle for territory, but a raid on a column of migrants strung out across the desert.

Deuteronomy supplies the detail Exodus leaves out. Amalek 'met you on your journey when you were tired and weary, and they attacked all your stragglers; they had no fear of God,' Deuteronomy 25:18. The rear of a travelling people held the old, the sick, the mothers with small children and the slowest animals. To strike there was to prey on the helpless, and ancient hearers would have heard it as a breach of every decency owed to travellers.

The exact location of Rephidim is not certain; the text places it on the route between the Desert of Sin and the Wilderness of Sinai, Exodus 17:1 and 19:2, near Horeb, 17:6. The staff in Moses' hand is the one he carried back to Egypt as 'the staff of God,' Exodus 4:20, stretched out over the sea and toward heaven in the plagues, Exodus 9:23 and 14:16. Raised or spread hands were also the ordinary posture of prayer in Israel, Exodus 9:29, 1 Kings 8:22 and Psalm 28:2, so an Israelite watching the hilltop would have seen both a sign of God's power and a man in prayer.

The written record matters too. Israel later cited a 'Book of the Wars of the LORD,' Numbers 21:14, and the command to write this battle down belongs to that instinct: the victories of God are to be kept in writing and read aloud to the next leader.
context.canonical:
The sentence on Amalek runs through the rest of the Old Testament. Balaam, looking out over the nations, says, 'Amalek was first among the nations, but his end is destruction,' Numbers 24:20. When Israel refuses to enter the land and then tries to fight without the LORD, it is the Amalekites and Canaanites who rout them 'all the way to Hormah,' Numbers 14:43-45. That scene is the dark mirror of Rephidim: there the LORD fought and Israel won, here Moses and the ark stay in the camp and Israel is beaten.

Moses charges Israel to remember what Amalek did, Deuteronomy 25:17-19, and the Amalekites keep appearing as raiders in the days of the judges, Judges 3:13 and 6:3. Saul is sent to carry out the sentence and spares Agag king of Amalek, 1 Samuel 15:2-3 and 15:8, and the failure is named again when his kingdom is taken, 1 Samuel 28:18. David recovers his families from an Amalekite raid on Ziklag, 1 Samuel 30, and an Amalekite brings him Saul's crown, 2 Samuel 1:8-10. The last of the Amalekites are struck down in the days of Hezekiah, 1 Chronicles 4:43, and Psalm 83:7 still lists Amalek among the nations that plot to erase Israel's name.

Many readers hear a final echo in Esther, where the enemy of the Jews is 'Haman son of Hammedatha, the Agagite,' Esther 3:1 and 9:24, a name that recalls Agag, the Amalekite king Saul spared.

The New Testament does not quote this passage, but it takes up both of its main figures. The name Joshua comes into Greek as Jesus, and Hebrews 4:8 and Acts 7:45 use the one name for both men. And the picture of a mediator lifting his hands for the people on the hill finds its fulfilment in the Christ who 'always lives to intercede,' Hebrews 7:25.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Moses wrote this for a people who would spend forty years in the desert and then fight for the land, and he wanted them to grasp how battles are won in the service of God. The staff of God, not Joshua's sword, decides the day, yet Joshua still has to choose men and go out. Israel was not to imagine that prayer made fighting unnecessary, nor that fighting could succeed without the LORD. The scene in Numbers 14:44-45, when Israel went up without Moses and without the ark and was beaten by the same enemy, shows how seriously that lesson was meant.

He also wanted Israel to see that the one who stands between them and God is himself weak. Moses tires, sits on a stone and has to be held up. Leadership in Israel would always depend on others who came alongside, and the rest of the wilderness story keeps returning to that theme, beginning with the very next chapter.

Finally, the command to write and recite was meant to form a memory. The LORD's word about Amalek was placed in writing and in Joshua's ears so that future generations would know who their enemies were, who had fought for them, and that God does not forget what is done to the weak among His people.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The passage describes one battle and records one divine sentence on one people. It does not command believers to raise their arms in a particular way in order to secure victory, and it does not turn prayer into a technique whose posture controls the outcome. The Mishnah already warned against that reading, asking whether Moses' hands made war, and answering that Israel prevailed when they looked upward and set their hearts on their Father in heaven.

Nor does the sentence on Amalek license violence today. It was spoken by God, tied to a specific act, and carried out, when it was carried out, by Israel as a nation under direct command. The church's warfare is 'not against flesh and blood,' Ephesians 6:12.

What does carry forward is the shape of the scene: faithful action and persevering prayer held together; a leader who needs and accepts support; companions who hold up weary hands, Galatians 6:2; and the settled confidence that the battle belongs to the LORD, 1 Samuel 17:47.

debates.question: How should Christians read the LORD's declared, generational war against Amalek and its later outworking under Saul?

views.label: As specific, time-bound covenant judgment
views.case: This is a particular sentence on a particular nation for a particular act, attacking the weary and the stragglers, Deuteronomy 25:18. It is executed within Israel's own redemptive history, by divine command through a prophet, 1 Samuel 15:2-3, and it is not a template for later warfare. God's judgments in the Old Testament often come after long patience, and here the sentence waited centuries before it fell.

views.label: As a picture of God's settled opposition to all that opposes His purposes
views.case: Others read Amalek typologically, as the first of the nations to strike at the redeemed, Numbers 24:20, and so a figure for every persistent enmity against God's people. On this view the final answer is not Israel's sword but Christ's reign until every enemy is under His feet, 1 Corinthians 15:25.

views.label: As a hard text to be held with moral seriousness
views.case: Many readers acknowledge the real moral weight of the command in 1 Samuel 15:3 and refuse to soften it. They note that the Kenites were warned and spared, 1 Samuel 15:6, that the sentence was on a people with a long history of preying on the defenceless, and that Scripture itself treats such judgment as God's prerogative alone, Deuteronomy 32:35.

debates.bearing: The text does not license personal vengeance or holy war today. It shows that God sees and remembers cruelty to the weak, that His justice may wait but does not lapse, and that its final execution belongs to Him, at the cross and at the last judgment.

debates.question: What does the obscure saying of verse 16, 'a hand was lifted up toward the throne of the LORD,' mean?

views.label: Moses' hand raised in oath
views.case: A raised hand is the gesture of swearing, and God Himself swears this way, 'I lift up My hand to heaven and declare,' Deuteronomy 32:40. On this reading Moses, or the LORD, takes an oath by the throne that the war against Amalek will continue from generation to generation. The BSB rendering leans this way.

views.label: Amalek's hand raised against God's throne
views.case: Others read the line as the charge against Amalek: a hand was lifted against the throne of the LORD, so the LORD will war against Amalek. The attack on Israel was in reality an attack on God's own rule, which explains why the sentence is so severe.

views.label: A banner, not a throne
views.case: The word for throne here, kes, is an unusual short form. Because the altar has just been named with nes, banner, many scholars suggest the original read 'a hand upon the banner of the LORD,' linking the saying to the altar's name. It is a scholarly conjecture rather than a settled reading, so it should be held loosely.

debates.bearing: Each reading ends in the same place: the conflict is the LORD's own, and He commits Himself to it. Whether the hand is Moses' oath or Amalek's defiance, the war is fought for the throne of God, and He will see it through.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 12 says that Moses' hands 'grew heavy.' The adjective is kaved, the same root the plague narrative used for Pharaoh's heart that was 'hardened,' literally made heavy, Exodus 9:7 and 9:34. The root also gives kavod, glory, and God said He would 'gain honor,' be glorified, through Pharaoh, Exodus 14:4. Heaviness in Exodus can mean stubbornness, weight of glory or, here, simple human fatigue. The prophet of God is no less mortal than anyone else.

The same verse ends by saying his hands 'remained steady until the sun went down.' The word for steady is emunah, a noun that usually means faithfulness or firmness. Moses' hands were, quite literally, faithfulness. It is the word of Habakkuk 2:4, 'the righteous will live by faith,' and of Psalm 89:8, where the LORD's faithfulness surrounds Him. What holds firm on the hill is not Moses' strength but a steadiness supplied by others and sustained by God.

The two verbs of the battle deserve notice. 'Prevailed' in verse 11 is gabar, the root behind gibbor, a mighty man or warrior; it is used for Israel and then for Amalek in turn, so that strength visibly passes back and forth with Moses' hands. In verse 13 Joshua 'overwhelmed' Amalek, from chalash, to weaken or lay low, the verb Isaiah 14:12 uses of the king of Babylon as a 'destroyer of nations.' The word suggests the enemy was broken rather than annihilated, which fits the later history.

Verse 14 is dense with memory words. Moses is to write it as a 'reminder,' zikkaron, because the LORD will blot out the 'memory,' zeker, of Amalek. The two nouns come from the same root, zakar, to remember, so that the memorial of Amalek is kept precisely in order to record the erasing of Amalek's memory. The verb 'blot out' is machah, the verb of the flood, 'I will blot out man,' Genesis 6:7, and it comes here in the emphatic doubled form, 'blotting out I will blot out,' which the BSB renders 'utterly blot out.'

The altar's name uses nes, banner or standard, the pole raised on a height so that scattered troops could rally, Jeremiah 51:27. Isaiah turns it into a messianic word: 'the Root of Jesse will stand as a banner for the peoples,' Isaiah 11:10. The same word names the pole on which Moses raised the bronze serpent, Numbers 21:8-9. The BSB footnote gives the Hebrew form of the name, YHWH Nissi. Exodus has already added a name of this kind, 'I am the LORD who heals you,' Exodus 15:26; now the LORD is named again by what He has done.

Finally, Joshua's name, Yehoshua, joins the divine name to the verb for saving. He is still called Hoshea in Numbers 13:16, where Moses is said to give him the longer name. In the Greek Old Testament the name is rendered Iesous, the same name the angel gives to Mary's son, 'because He will save His people from their sins,' Matthew 1:21.

typology.type: Moses on the hill with lifted hands, held up by Aaron and Hur
typology.fulfillment: A mediator stands above the battle while the people fight below, and the outcome depends on his lifted hands. Christ fulfils the pattern in a higher key. He is seated at the right hand of God and 'is interceding for us,' Romans 8:34, and 'always lives to intercede' for those who come to God through Him, Hebrews 7:25. Where Moses' hands grew heavy by afternoon, the LORD 'will not grow tired or weary,' Isaiah 40:28. The type falls short at its most touching point: Moses needed Aaron and Hur, but Christ needs no one to hold Him up, and it is He who holds up His people.

typology.type: Joshua, the saviour-named captain, fighting below
typology.fulfillment: Joshua makes his first appearance as the one who leads Israel's men into battle, the same role he will fill when he brings Israel into the land. His name, meaning that the LORD saves, is the Hebrew form of Jesus, and Hebrews 4:8 uses the one name for both. Jesus is the greater Joshua, who fights the decisive battle against sin, death and the devil, Colossians 2:15. Yet the correspondence breaks: Joshua won under another's intercession and could not give Israel lasting rest, Hebrews 4:8, while Jesus both wins the battle and intercedes, and gives a rest that remains, Hebrews 4:9.

typology.type: The banner raised over the battlefield, The LORD Is My Banner
typology.fulfillment: The altar names the LORD Himself as the standard around which Israel rallied. The same word, nes, names the pole on which the bronze serpent was lifted so that the dying could look and live, Numbers 21:8-9, and Jesus applies that scene to His own lifting up on the cross, John 3:14-15. Isaiah promises that the Root of Jesse will stand as a banner for the peoples, Isaiah 11:10. The escalation is that the banner is no longer a pole or an altar but a person, lifted up to draw all people to Himself, John 12:32. This is a link of shared imagery, not a declared New Testament type, and should be held lightly.

typology.type: Outstretched arms from morning until sunset
typology.fulfillment: Early Christian writers such as Justin Martyr and the Epistle of Barnabas saw in Moses' arms stretched out until sunset a figure of the cross, where Christ's arms were stretched out and the enemy was defeated. The New Testament never makes the connection, so it should be treated as an echo noticed by devout readers rather than a teaching of the text. What the New Testament does say is that through the cross Christ disarmed the powers and triumphed over them, Colossians 2:15, a victory won not while His hands were held up by others but while they were nailed.

study.christ:
The passage leads to Christ first through its two central figures, and it helps to keep them distinct. On the hill is a mediator whose lifted hands decide the battle. In the valley is a captain named Joshua who fights it. In the Old Testament these are two men, and neither can do the other's work. In Christ they become one person. He is the captain who goes into the battle Himself and the intercessor whose prayer never fails.

The intercession is the point the New Testament presses most. Christ Jesus 'who died, and more than that was raised to life, is at the right hand of God, and He is interceding for us,' Romans 8:34. He 'always lives to intercede' for those who draw near through Him, Hebrews 7:25. That is not only a heavenly office. On the night He was betrayed He told Peter, 'I have prayed for you, Simon, that your faith will not fail,' Luke 22:32, and He prayed for His disciples, 'keep them from the evil one,' John 17:15. The disciples fought their battles in the valley that night, and lost them for a time, but the prayer above them held.

The battle is the second point. Joshua fought flesh and blood. Christ fought the enemy behind every enemy. At the cross He 'disarmed the powers and authorities' and 'made a public spectacle of them', Colossians 2:15, and He now reigns 'until He has put all His enemies under His feet,' 1 Corinthians 15:25. The enemy that preyed on Israel's weakest at the rear of the column is a fitting picture of one who attacks the weak and weary, and Christ is the Shepherd who gathers those very stragglers, Isaiah 40:11.

The passage also leads to Christ by contrast. Moses' hands grew heavy by afternoon; the Protector of Israel 'will neither slumber nor sleep,' Psalm 121:4. Moses needed a stone and two friends; Christ bore the full weight alone and then shares His victory with His people. When He was lifted up it was not on a hilltop above the fight but on a cross in the middle of it, and the victory came through His wounds rather than in spite of them.

There is also a word here for the church. The New Testament keeps the pattern of Aaron and Hur alive among believers. Paul asks the Romans to 'join me in my struggle by praying to God for me,' Romans 15:30, and Epaphras is 'always wrestling in prayer' for the Colossians, Colossians 4:12. Those prayers are never the ground of victory, which is Christ's alone, but they are the way Christ's people share in His work.

A caution keeps the reading honest. The New Testament does not quote Exodus 17, and not every detail is a hidden picture of Jesus; the stone Moses sat on is a stone. The links rest on the names, the offices and the explicit teaching about Christ's intercession and reign. Read that way, Rephidim becomes a small, true window onto the whole work of Christ, who fights for His people and prays for them at once.
study.god:
The first thing this passage shows about God is that He answers the question His people asked in doubt. At Massah they said, 'Is the LORD among us or not?' Exodus 17:7. He does not reply with a lecture. He replies by fighting for them the next day. His presence is proved not by removing every enemy but by standing with His people when the enemy comes.

He is the warrior God of the Song of the Sea, 'The LORD is a warrior, the LORD is His name,' Exodus 15:3, and yet the way He fights changes here. At the sea He told Israel, 'The LORD will fight for you; you need only to be still,' Exodus 14:14. At Rephidim Israel must choose men and take up swords. God is sovereign in both battles, but He is pleased to work through human action as well as without it. His sovereignty does not make obedience pointless; it makes obedience fruitful.

He is also the God who binds His power to prayer. The swing of the battle with Moses' hands is not magic, and it is not a sign that God depends on Moses. It is a lesson in which the LORD ties the visible outcome to the posture of dependence so that no one could miss where the victory came from. The same God who could have routed Amalek in a moment chose to teach His people to pray.

He is just, and His justice remembers. The sentence on Amalek is severe, and it is not arbitrary. Deuteronomy gives the reason: they attacked the tired and weary and 'had no fear of God,' Deuteronomy 25:18. God's attention to the stragglers at the back of the column is a quiet revelation of His heart. The people others treat as expendable are the ones He takes most personally. Yet His justice is not hasty. The war runs 'from generation to generation,' verse 16, and when the sentence finally falls under Saul, the Kenites are warned and spared, 1 Samuel 15:6. Judgment is measured, patient and discriminating.

He is faithful to His own word. He tells Moses to write it down and to recite it to Joshua, binding Himself to a promise in writing. Samuel later says that 'the Glory of Israel does not lie or change His mind,' 1 Samuel 15:29, precisely in the context of this sentence.

And He is the God who gives Himself a name through what He does. After Marah He was 'the LORD who heals you,' Exodus 15:26; after Rephidim He is The LORD Is My Banner. Worship in Israel grows out of history. For believers the right response is to rally where He has planted the standard, to keep praying when the arms grow heavy, and to give the credit where Moses gave it, on an altar and not on a monument to Joshua.

crossReferences.note: Moses' later sermon fills in what Exodus leaves unsaid: Amalek struck when Israel was 'tired and weary,' attacking the stragglers, and 'they had no fear of God.' It also sets the timing of the sentence, once the LORD has given Israel rest in the land, and ends with the blunt charge, 'Do not forget!'

The reverse of Rephidim. When Israel tries to take the land after refusing it, Moses warns that the LORD is not among them, and neither Moses nor the ark leaves the camp. The same Amalekites rout them. Victory in Exodus 17 was never Joshua's skill; without the LORD the same army loses.

Balaam's oracle calls Amalek 'first among the nations,' probably meaning first to attack Israel, as at Rephidim, and declares that 'his end is destruction.' The sentence spoken to Moses in Exodus 17:14 is confirmed by a foreign prophet under God's constraint.

Centuries later the LORD of Hosts says, 'I witnessed what the Amalekites did to the Israelites when they ambushed them on their way up from Egypt,' and sends Saul to carry out the sentence. Saul's partial obedience, sparing Agag, costs him the kingdom, 1 Samuel 15:23, and shows that the war 'from generation to generation' was real.

Haman is introduced as 'the Agagite,' a title that recalls Agag king of Amalek, 1 Samuel 15:8. Many readers see the book of Esther as the last chapter of the conflict begun at Rephidim, with an enemy once more seeking to destroy the whole people and God once more preserving them.

Christ 'always lives to intercede' for those who draw near to God through Him. Moses interceded on the hill for a single day and needed help to keep going; the risen Christ intercedes without end and so is able to save completely. Rephidim shows the need, Hebrews shows the answer.

Paul places Christ 'at the right hand of God' where 'He is interceding for us.' The mediator is not on a hilltop within sight of the battle but at the throne of God itself, the very throne toward which the hand of Exodus 17:16 was lifted.

The LORD 'will not grow tired or weary,' and He 'gives power to the faint.' Moses' heavy hands show the limit of every human mediator; Isaiah promises that the God who never tires renews the strength of those who wait on Him, so that they can run and not grow weary.

The same word as the altar's name, nes, is the pole on which Moses mounted the bronze serpent so that the bitten could look and live. Jesus takes up that scene in John 3:14-15. The LORD who was Israel's banner in battle becomes the one lifted up for healing.

David tells Goliath that 'it is not by sword or spear that the LORD saves; for the battle is the LORD's.' Joshua's sword was real at Rephidim, but David states the lesson the altar's name was meant to teach: human weapons are instruments, and the LORD alone is the victor.

Epaphras is 'always wrestling in prayer' for the Colossians so that they may stand firm. The New Testament keeps the pattern of Aaron and Hur alive: believers hold up one another's hands in prayer while the struggle goes on, sharing under Christ in the work He alone completes.

Christ 'must reign until He has put all His enemies under His feet.' The war 'from generation to generation' in Exodus 17:16 finds its end not in any single battle but in the reign of the risen Christ, which will leave no enemy of God's people standing.

study.oneStory:
In Genesis God promised Abraham, 'I will bless those who bless you and curse those who curse you,' Genesis 12:3. Exodus 17 and 18 show that promise at work within a single week. Amalek, descended from Esau, the brother who despised his birthright, attacks the redeemed and comes under a curse. Jethro, a Midianite, comes to bless and shares a meal before God. The nations are already dividing around the people God has chosen.

The passage also answers something older. Since Genesis 3:15 Scripture has spoken of enmity between two seeds. Amalek is the first nation to strike at Israel after the exodus, and Balaam calls it 'first among the nations,' Numbers 24:20. The long war it begins runs through Saul and David to Haman in Esther, a reminder that the rescued people live in a world where the ancient hostility is still active.

Within the exodus story itself Rephidim marks a turn. At the sea Israel only watched. Here Israel fights, and learns that God's victories come through obedience joined to prayer. That lesson will be needed at Jericho and throughout the conquest, where Joshua, trained here, leads. Yet the rest he gives is not final, Hebrews 4:8, and Israel's later history shows how often the lesson was forgotten, beginning with Numbers 14.

The story comes to rest in Christ, who unites in one person what was divided at Rephidim. He is the Joshua who wins the battle and the mediator whose intercession never tires. At the cross the enemy behind every Amalek was disarmed, Colossians 2:15, and now the risen Christ reigns until every enemy is under His feet, 1 Corinthians 15:25. Meanwhile His people live between the victory and its completion, fighting real battles, holding up one another's hands in prayer, and rallying to the banner He has raised.

The new creation is the war's end. The last enemy, death, is destroyed, 1 Corinthians 15:26. There will be no more raiders at the rear of the column, because the weakest will be gathered in and the tired and weary will be given rest. The God who wrote a war into a scroll will one day write a peace that never ends, and His people will see the throne toward which Moses lifted his hand, the throne of God and of the Lamb, Revelation 22:3.

quiz.q: Why did Amalek's attack on Israel deserve special condemnation, according to Deuteronomy 25:17-18?

options.text: Because Amalek struck the weary and straggling from behind, attacking those too exhausted to defend themselves.
options.note: Deuteronomy 25:17-18 gives this exact reason for Amalek's lasting condemnation.

options.text: Because Amalek refused to let Israel pass through their territory.
options.note: That is the complaint against Edom and others, not the specific charge against Amalek here.

options.text: Because Amalek worshiped different gods than Israel.
options.note: The stated reason is Amalek's cruelty toward the weary and defenseless, not a dispute over worship.

options.text: No reason for the attack is ever given in Scripture.
options.note: Deuteronomy 25:17-18 explicitly explains why Amalek's attack was so condemned.

quiz.q: What determined whether Israel or Amalek prevailed in the battle?

options.text: Whether Moses kept his hands lifted up; Israel prevailed when they were up and Amalek prevailed when they were down.
options.note: Verse 11 states this directly.

options.text: The number of soldiers Joshua chose to fight.
options.note: The text ties the outcome to Moses' hands, not the size of Joshua's force.

options.text: The time of day the battle was fought.
options.note: Time of day is not what the text credits; it is Moses' lifted hands.

options.text: The battle's outcome had nothing to do with Moses at all.
options.note: The text ties the outcome directly and repeatedly to Moses' raised hands.

quiz.q: Who helped Moses when his hands grew heavy, and how?

options.text: Aaron and Hur, who held his hands up on each side until sunset while he sat on a stone.
options.note: Verse 12 describes this exactly.

options.text: Joshua, who left the battle to come and help him.
options.note: Joshua remained in the battle below; Aaron and Hur held up Moses' hands.

options.text: The elders of Israel, who prayed at the base of the hill.
options.note: The text names Aaron and Hur specifically as the ones who held up Moses' hands.

options.text: No one helped Moses; he held his own hands up unaided the entire day.
options.note: Verse 12 explicitly says Aaron and Hur held his hands up.

quiz.q: What did Moses name the altar he built after the victory, and why?

options.text: The LORD Is My Banner, giving credit for the victory to God rather than to Israel's own strength.
options.note: Verse 15 records this name directly.

options.text: Ebenezer, marking a stone of help.
options.note: Ebenezer belongs to a later victory in 1 Samuel 7, not to this altar.

options.text: Bethel, the house of God.
options.note: Bethel is the name Jacob gave a different site in Genesis, not this altar.

options.text: The altar was left unnamed in the text.
options.note: Verse 15 explicitly gives the altar's name.

quiz.q: What did the LORD declare regarding Amalek in verses 14 and 16?

options.text: That He would utterly blot out the memory of Amalek and would war against Amalek from generation to generation.
options.note: Verses 14 and 16 state this declaration directly.

options.text: That Amalek would be shown mercy and welcomed into Israel.
options.note: The declaration is one of lasting judgment, the opposite of welcome or mercy.

options.text: That Amalek's descendants would become priests in Israel.
options.note: No such role is given to Amalek; the declared word is one of judgment.

options.text: That the LORD would never mention Amalek again.
options.note: The opposite is true; Moses is told to write this down precisely so it will be remembered.

questions: Amalek attacked Israel at their weariest and most vulnerable moment. Where do you find yourself most vulnerable to spiritual attack right now, and how are you guarding that place?
Israel's victory needed both Joshua's sword and Moses' lifted hands; neither alone was enough. Where might you be relying only on effort, or only on prayer, when God calls you to both?
Moses grew weary and needed Aaron and Hur to hold up his hands. Who holds up your hands when you grow weary in prayer or service, and whose hands are you holding up?
Moses named the altar for God's help, not Israel's strength. What victory in your own life do you need to rename, giving credit to God rather than to yourself?

The text is honest that God's judgment on Amalek would take generations to complete. How do you hold onto trust in God's justice when His timing for setting things right is far slower than you would like?

translationNotes.note: The staff of God is the same staff Moses used to strike the Nile and the rock, Exodus 7:20, 17:6; carrying it up the hill ties this battle to the same divine power at work in Israel's earlier deliverances.

The LORD Is My Banner renders the Hebrew Yahweh Nissi; a nes was a raised standard or rallying signal, so the name declares that God Himself, not Israel's army, was the true rallying point of the victory.

The closing line is one of the most compressed and debated in the Hebrew Bible, literally a hand upon the kes, a shortened form of throne, of Yah, a shortened form of the divine name; translators have long wrestled with its exact grammar, but its sense, that this war belongs to the LORD across generations, is clear.
